Grande Chartreuse
grahnd shar-TRERZ
n. (the mother house of the Carthusian order, founded by Bruno in 1084 in the Chartreuse massif)
French, the great Chartreuse, from the valley of Chartreuse in Dauphiné; Latin Cartusia.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Grande Chartreuse stands at a thousand metres in a closed valley of the Chartreuse massif north of Grenoble, and has been the head of the Carthusian order since Bruno settled there in 1084. The present buildings date largely from after the fire of 1676, one of some eight fires and avalanches that have destroyed the house; the great cloister is the longest in France, running past the separate cells of the fathers. The monks have made the liqueur since the eighteenth century from a recipe only two of them know, which funds the order. No visitors are admitted. This dictionary records the Grande Chartreuse for the silence it keeps, because stillness in Scripture is commanded in a particular connection. It is the posture before God himself, “Be still, and know that I am God” (Psa 46:10). It is the whole earth's proper attitude, “let all the earth keep silence before him” (Hab 2:20). It is where Elijah finally heard what he came for, “and after the fire a still small voice” (1Ki 19:12), and it is where strength is said to be found, “in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength” (Isa 30:15).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines silence as forbearance of speech; stillness as freedom from noise; quietness as rest or repose; solitude as a lonely life; and a cell as a small close apartment.

expand to see more

SILENCE, n. Forbearance of speech in man; taciturnity; omission of speech; also, stillness; the state of being without sound.

STILLNESS, n. Freedom from noise or motion; calmness; quiet; silence.

QUIETNESS, n. A state of rest; stillness; calmness; freedom from agitation or alarm; tranquillity; peace.

SOLITUDE, n. Loneliness; a state of being alone; a lonely life; also, a lonely place; a desert.

CELL, n. A small or close apartment, as in a prison; also, a small cave or hollow place; the cave or hut of a hermit.

Key Scripture

Psa 46:10 — "Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth."

Hab 2:20 — "But the LORD is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him."

1Ki 19:12 — "And after the earthquake a fire; but the LORD was not in the fire: and after the fire a still small voice."

Isa 30:15 — "For thus saith the Lord GOD, the Holy One of Israel; In returning and rest shall ye be saved; in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength: and ye would not."

Modern Corruption

Mother house of the Carthusians, 1084: eight times destroyed by fire and avalanche, rebuilt each time, and closed to visitors still.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture commands stillness and attaches it to knowing God rather than to emptying the mind, “Be still, and know that I am God” (Psa 46:10). Habakkuk makes it the creation's proper posture rather than a technique, “But the LORD is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him” (Hab 2:20). Modern life is loud and the correction is biblical, not merely monastic.

The qualification is in Elijah's case, which is the passage most often cited and most often truncated. He did not go to the mountain for silence; he went in despair, and the silence was the setting in which a voice spoke and gave him orders, “and after the fire a still small voice” (1Ki 19:12). The quietness Isaiah commends is likewise a confidence in someone, and the verse ends with Israel refusing it, “in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength” (Isa 30:15). Silence is a room, not an answer.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew raphah (H7503), to be still; Hebrew damam (H1826), to be silent; Hebrew demamah (H1827), a stillness; Hebrew shaqat (H8252), to be quiet; Hebrew bitchah (H985), confidence.

expand to see more

Hebrew raphah (H7503) — to let go, to be still; “Be still, and know that I am God”, Psalm 46:10.

Hebrew damam (H1826) — to be silent before him; “let all the earth keep silence before him”, Habakkuk 2:20.

Hebrew demamah (H1827) — a calm, a still whisper; “and after the fire a still small voice”, 1 Kings 19:12.

Hebrew shuqat — from shaqat (H8252), to be at rest; “in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength”, Isaiah 30:15.

Hebrew heykal (H1964) — a temple, where the LORD is; “But the LORD is in his holy temple”, Habakkuk 2:20.

Usage

"“Be still, and know that I am God” (Psa 46:10) — stillness attached to knowing, not emptying."

"“and after the fire a still small voice” (1Ki 19:12) — the silence was the room, not the answer."

"“in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength” (Isa 30:15) — and they refused it."
